articles.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
articles.dek: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0. 4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new…
paragraphs: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0. 4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data .

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget projects 38. 2 billion metric tons of fossil carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions this year. Emissions from oil are projected to decrease by 1. 9%—likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict.

While global energy demand continues to rise, two-thirds of the increase is being met by increased solar and wind power and electric vehicles. However, the report finds that clean energy growth is not yet fast enough for a durable decline in global fossil CO₂ emissions.

With emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) projected to increase slightly this year, total CO₂ emissions are projected to be 43. 3 billion metric tons in 2026—up from 42. 8 billion metric tons last year.

The remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO₂ that can be emitted before warming reaches 1. 5°C above preindustrial levels) is now 150 billion metric tons—equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.
With CO₂ still rapidly accumulating in the atmosphere, the dangerous impacts of climate change continue to increase.

The report also assesses natural "sinks" (absorption of CO₂ by land and ocean). It finds that the land sink returned to former levels after a severe weakening during the 2023–24 El Niño weather pattern.
However, the powerful 2026 El Niño is expected to have a significant impact in the coming year.

The research team included the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), Alfred-Wegener-Institut and more than 90 other institutions around the world.

"A decline in fossil CO₂ emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution," said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline."

Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society research professor at UEA's School of Environmental Sciences, said, "Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years."

Glen Peters, research professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, said, "A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles is pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions."

Professor Julia Pongratz, at LMU's Department of Geography, said, "Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO₂ removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO₂, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now."

articles.title: The surprising power of connecting with strangers
articles.dek: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style.
paragraphs: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed.
You pass by an older woman on the way out, steeling yourself for judgment.
Instead, you get a knowing smile and hear, "We've all been there. You're doing great, Mama."

These commonplace moments with a stranger can make all the difference in helping someone feel like they belong, but until recently, these sparks of connection didn't have a name. Now, thanks to a University of Georgia researcher, they do: evanescent interactions . The article was published in Theory and Society .

"What is communicated by these evanescent interactions is essentially, 'You've noticed me. You've confirmed my existence. You've communicated that I am welcome here, that I belong here, that I have a place here, that I have value,'" said Joseph Hermanowicz, author of the publication and a professor of sociology in UGA's Franklin College of Arts and Sciences.
Hermanowicz defines evanescent interactions as brief moments when "strangers exchange gestures that create a 'spark' between them."
An evanescent interaction is more than just an ordinary exchange of pleasantries.
These moments consist of brief but meaningful exchanges of mutual understanding and connection.

"It's important to be pleasant and kind to people, particularly in our present times, of course," Hermanowicz said. "But I think it's also important to recognize that when we do have a certain deliberateness with communicating with people, we could be accomplishing something very meaningful. We could communicate to people that they are important, that they matter, that we together form a community."
In his earlier research on the causes of undergraduate attrition, Hermanowicz found that evanescent interactions often influenced whether a student stuck it out or dropped out.
Former students who dropped out said that a meaningful encounter with someone at the university who showed genuine interest in their well-being might have helped them feel more like they belonged.
"In the absence of such contact, they felt alienated and not noticed, which fueled or did not impede a desire to leave," he said. "So they left.

"A lot of people are lonely. These sparks of connection can thwart feelings of not belonging in the various groups and organizations that we are a part of, whether those are friendship groups, work organizations or society more broadly."
Evanescent interactions are brief, positive and highly emotionally charged. They're so ordinary that people may not give them a second thought.

articles.title: Gatineau Park foliage reveals local Cold War nuclear testing legacy
articles.dek: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record…
paragraphs: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record of its kind. Now, a study of those leaves led by the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AEL-AMS) located at the University of Ottawa shows that the effects of Cold War–era nuclear weapons testing have only recently disappeared from the local biosphere. The study, titled " Stored carbohydrates buffer Bomb and Suess radiocarbon effects in maple leaves across a 65-year Ottawa region record ," was published in Scientific Reports .

The Geological Survey of Canada began collecting maple leaves in Gatineau Park in 1961, taking samples once a month during each growing season. Its scientists analyzed the leaves until the agency's radiocarbon laboratory closed in 2004. The AEL-AMS later took over the analyses and extended the record through 2025, adding 59 annual and seasonal measurements. The collection is ongoing, though leaves gathered in September 2026 are not included in the current study.

"These leaves are a 65-year diary of the atmosphere," explains Dr. Leonard Wassenaar, executive director of the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) at the University of Ottawa. "It took more than 65 years for the extra radiocarbon from weapons testing to disappear from the Ottawa-area biosphere. The effects were still with us decades after the last test."

Because leaves absorb carbon dioxide that is turned into sugars used for the tree's growth, the radiocarbon in each leaf sample preserves information about the atmosphere at the time. The Gatineau Park collection gave researchers an unusually detailed picture of how atmospheric radiocarbon changed from the height of Cold War weapons testing to the present day.

Above-ground nuclear tests conducted in the late 1950s and early 1960s, mostly by the United States and by the Soviet Union but also by the U. K. , France and China, released large amounts of radiocarbon into the atmosphere, roughly doubling global levels. Scientists refer to this sharp increase as the "bomb pulse."

In leaves from the Ottawa region, the signal peaked in 1964 at 842 parts per thousand above the reference level. By 2025, it had fallen to –13. 9 parts per thousand. That decline happened for two main reasons. Oceans gradually absorbed much of the excess radiocarbon, while emissions from burning coal, oil and natural gas diluted it. Fossil fuels are so old that the carbon dioxide they produce contains virtually no radiocarbon.
Direct air measurements show atmospheric radiocarbon dropped below its pre-bomb baseline around 2021–2022, but local maple leaves crossed that threshold in 2024.

Researchers often use radiocarbon in leaves and tree rings to reconstruct past atmospheric conditions. These studies usually assume that a sample reflects the atmosphere in the year it grew. But these new findings show that the picture is slightly more complicated. Plants do not build new growth entirely from carbon absorbed that same year. They can also draw on carbon stored during previous growing seasons.

The researchers found that sugar maple leaves closely follow changes in atmospheric radiocarbon, but lag behind by about 2. 2 years, with a margin of uncertainty of 0. 3 years. The leaves also showed a small positive offset that averaged 7. 4 parts per thousand between 1990 and 2019.

"Plants often use older carbon, stored from previous years, to grow new leaves," adds Wassenaar. "We didn't know how much that changed a leaf's radiocarbon signature, or whether leaves tracked the atmosphere consistently. Now we do."
These findings give scientists a more accurate way to interpret radiocarbon measurements from preserved leaves, tree rings and other plant material.

"Leaves are a reliable way to reconstruct atmospheric radiocarbon from places and periods we never measured directly," concludes Wassenaar. "Once you factor in the two-year delay, our interpretations should be more precise."
The leaves were collected with permission from the National Capital Commission.

articles.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
articles.dek: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an…
paragraphs: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors.

The engineers found that pressing a fine diamond tip a few nanometers into molybdenum can reform the crystals inside molybdenum, giving the metal new properties. The results, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , took the researchers by surprise.

"We had a hypothesis that applying extreme pressure to molybdenum would cause it to transform to a new solid phase," says associate professor Niaz Abdolrahim from URochester's Department of Mechanical Engineering. "But then we found this interesting phenomenon of an entirely different stress-driven mechanism."

Abdolrahim says that while metals look uniform to the naked eye, zooming in on their microstructures reveals that they are made of many small atomic regions called crystal grains. Changing the shape, orientation and size of crystal grains redefines how a material behaves—affecting things like its strength and malleability. And normally, molybdenum's crystal grains cannot be changed—or recrystallized—until it is heated to about 1,000°C (1,832°F).

Through experiments and computer modeling, the researchers found that molybdenum can be recrystallized at room temperature using a tiny, calibrated probe called a nanoindenter, which has a diamond tip that is used to test material properties. But recrystallization requires precision. Just a little force from the nanoindenter creates extreme pressure that causes the diamond tip to push through the metal's surface in a quick movement known as a "pop-in." Entering this pop-in phase causes the metal to recrystallize. But applying too much pressure—and moving past the pop-in phase—causes the new grains to disappear.

Manually stopping the test right after the pop-in event causes recrystallization in a tiny region surrounding the dent left in the material. Researchers say the technique can be useful for fixing defects within a larger sample of molybdenum, changing the properties of the defective area to the desired state without affecting the rest of the sample.

"Currently if you have a damaged sample, to fix it or form new grains, you have to heat the whole sample up to 1,000°C (1,832°F) or more," says Afnan Mostafa, a mechanical engineering Ph. D. student in Abdolrahim's lab. "Here we show you don't need to heat up the whole sample. You just need to know where to poke, how much and when to stop."

The researchers say semiconductor manufacturers are exploring molybdenum as a potential material for next-generation semiconductor interconnects, the tiny wires that connect millions of components on a microchip. As artificial intelligence systems demand more and more computing power, manufacturers are trying to make smaller and more powerful microchips. To achieve this, researchers are exploring replacing the copper in semiconductors with molybdenum.

"Copper usually has a resistance increase at nanoscales, which means electricity doesn't flow through it as well," says Mostafa. "Molybdenum doesn't have that problem, which makes it appealing for the next generation of tiny microchip interconnects."
But molybdenum currently has its own drawbacks, which the researchers' new technique may help address.

"While molybdenum is extremely durable at high temperatures, at room temperatures, it can snap without any warning that it's going to break," Mostafa says. "So, we want to explore if we can improve that. If we can find new ways to recrystallize the material at room temperature, it could give us new uses for molybdenum that are currently only available at high temperatures."

articles.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
articles.dek: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves…
paragraphs: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates.
Published in Science Advances , the study found that this difference affects how an Andes virus glycoprotein moves through human cells and how quickly virus-like particles are released.

Andes virus is a rodent-borne RNA virus that can cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome , a severe and potentially life-threatening illness. It was the virus involved in the fatal 2026 outbreak aboard the cruise ship Hondius. Unlike other known hantaviruses, Andes virus can spread from person to person. Understanding its biological behavior may help researchers investigate factors involved in human infection and transmission.

Researchers in the Palacios Lab at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai compared an Andes virus isolate from a rodent host with a human-derived isolate collected during the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina. That outbreak involved person-to-person transmission and resulted in 11 deaths. Previous research identified biological differences between the genetically similar isolates.

The researchers identified 25 amino acid differences between the isolates. They focused on one difference near a part of the virus known as the glycoprotein cleavage domain because of its potential relevance to glycoprotein processing and virus assembly.

The rodent-derived isolate grew faster than the human-derived isolate, although both eventually reached similar levels. After finding no major changes in viral RNA production that could explain the difference, the researchers investigated later stages of the viral life cycle. They changed one amino acid in the human-derived isolate's glycoprotein to match the rodent-derived version.
The modified protein spent less time in the Golgi apparatus, a cell compartment involved in protein processing, and virus-like particles were released more quickly.

"We still know relatively little about the viral features that may influence how Andes virus behaves in humans. What this study gives us is a specific molecular difference that we can connect to a measurable biological change. Understanding those connections is an important step toward identifying the viral features that may shape how these pathogens adapt, spread and cause disease," said corresponding author Gustavo Palacios, Ph. D. , professor of microbiology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.
The results provide a starting point for studying how genetic differences between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates affect viral biology.

The team used molecular expression systems and virus-like particles, not genetically modified infectious Andes virus. The results do not show that this amino acid change causes person-to-person transmission or adaptation to humans. Further research is needed to determine its effects in the complete virus and any relationship to disease or transmission.

"Among the differences between these two viruses, we focused on this particular change because of its location in a key viral protein. Understanding how such a small molecular difference can affect viral protein processing and the release of new viral particles could help identify new targets for antiviral therapies.

"It may also provide valuable insights into the molecular factors that contribute to differences in viral pathogenicity, ultimately helping guide future research toward better treatments," said first author Santiago Vidal-Freire, Ph. D. , an associate scientist and postdoctoral fellow in microbiology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.

The researchers also noted that viral sequences from the Hondius outbreak could support future studies. Using similar experimental systems, researchers could examine changes identified in the glycoprotein transmembrane domain of the Hondius isolate and assess their effects on viral protein behavior. Such studies may help clarify which molecular differences influence Andes virus biology.

articles.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
articles.dek: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators.
paragraphs: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear.

But Britain's breeding starling population has declined dramatically over recent decades, while changes in climate, migration and habitats are reshaping the lives of many birds. Could these wider changes also be affecting murmurations? By repeating a major citizen-science survey we carried out 12 years ago, we're hoping to find out whether these spectacular displays are changing in size, timing or location.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology , the U. K.' s breeding starling population declined by 61% between 1995 and 2024. This is part of a wider pattern of bird declines: the U. K.' s farmland bird population index has fallen by 62% since 1970 , with intensification of farming playing a major role.

But that doesn't necessarily mean individual murmurations are becoming smaller. Changes in where birds gather, when they arrive and how they behave could all influence the displays we see each winter.

Climate change may also be playing a part in shifting patterns and timings of murmuration displays. Britain's winter starling population includes large numbers of birds arriving from continental Europe . As winter conditions change, so might their migration patterns, potentially affecting the timing, location and size of murmurations. Changes in food availability and roosting habitat could also be important.

Our original citizen-science project began in 2014. Working with the Royal Society of Biology, we harnessed people power to record murmurations between 2014 and 2016. Volunteer citizen scientists submitted more than 3,000 observations, noting the size, duration and location of murmurations, plus the presence of any birds of prey. Observations from 23 countries provided an unusually large data set.

Back then, our main question wasn't whether murmurations were changing, but why they happened at all. Over the last 20 years, scientists have made considerable progress in understanding how thousands of birds coordinate their movements , with each responding to its neighbors to produce those extraordinary patterns. But why do starlings gather in such spectacular formations in the first place?

One explanation was that the displays helped attract birds to communal roosts, where gathering in large numbers might provide warmth. Another was that murmurations helped protect starlings from predators such as peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks. Moving together in a dense, constantly changing flock could make it harder for a predator to single out a specific bird, while providing more eyes to detect approaching danger.

Our findings, published in 2017 , provided strong support for this predator-avoidance explanation. Murmurations tended to be larger and last longer when predators were present, particularly when they approached or attacked the flock. Although we couldn't establish cause and effect from these observations alone, the evidence suggested that avoiding predators was a major reason for these spectacular displays, with attracting birds to a warm communal roost on cold nights being a secondary factor.

Our research also revealed a seasonal pattern in murmuration size and duration, with day length associated with how long displays lasted. Twelve years later, we are exploring whether those patterns have persisted, and whether the relationships between murmurations, predators and temperatures remain the same.

Once again, we're asking the public to help. By recording where and when they see murmurations, how many birds are involved, how long the displays last and whether predators are present, observers can help us investigate whether this extraordinary behavior is changing.

A starling murmuration isn't just a feast for the eyes. As the birds sweep low overhead, you can hear the collective rush of thousands of wings. And there's another sensory experience, too: a shower of starling droppings. Somehow, even that adds to the occasion, although we'd recommend taking an umbrella.

articles.title: Is Einstein Wrong? Deep-Sea Neutrinos Put the Laws of Physics to the Test
articles.dek: Scientists are testing whether one of Einstein’s most fundamental principles holds true throughout the Universe.
paragraphs: Scientists are testing whether one of Einstein’s most fundamental principles holds true throughout the Universe.

A neutrino telescope deep in the Mediterranean Sea has put one of Einstein’s fundamental principles to a new test. After analyzing 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events, scientists found no evidence that Lorentz invariance, a cornerstone of relativity, had been violated. Their findings place new restrictions on theories suggesting that the laws of physics might behave differently under certain conditions.

The international KM3NeT collaboration conducted the study using KM3NeT/ORCA, an underwater detector designed to investigate neutrinos and their unusual behavior. Published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), the research establishes the first direct experimental limits on certain possible violations involving muon and tau neutrinos, two types of these elusive particles.

Lorentz invariance requires the fundamental laws of physics to remain unchanged for observers moving at different constant velocities or facing different directions. Some theories of quantum gravity, which attempt to unite general relativity with quantum physics, suggest that this principle might not hold perfectly at extremely small scales.
One possibility is that spacetime is not truly continuous but consists of tiny, discrete units. If such a structure exists, it could produce subtle deviations from the predictions of relativity.

“We still don’t know whether our spacetime is continuous or might be discrete,” explains Alba Domi, a researcher at the Erlangen Center for Astroparticle Physics (ECAP), Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, and one of the study’s corresponding authors. “Looking for violations of Lorentz invariance is one way to investigate this possibility.”

Neutrinos are exceptionally difficult to detect because they interact so weakly with matter. Vast numbers pass through Earth without leaving a trace, allowing them to travel enormous distances with little interference.

These particles also possess an unusual ability: they can transform between different types, or “flavor” (this is the term used by scientists), as they travel. Known as neutrino oscillation, this phenomenon follows mathematical predictions that scientists can test against observations. Unexpected changes in these oscillations could indicate previously unknown physical effects, including violations of Lorentz invariance.

To search for such discrepancies, the researchers examined 1. 4 years of observations collected by KM3NeT/ORCA. At the time, the telescope was operating with only six detection units. The team compared the neutrinos’ measured energies and arrival directions with theoretical predictions to identify potential departures from established physics.

The analysis revealed no evidence of Lorentz invariance violation. However, it established tighter constraints on certain possible effects, including those that could influence oscillations between muon and tau neutrinos.

Despite relying on an early version of the detector, the results were competitive with measurements from established experiments such as IceCube and Super-Kamiokande, which have collected neutrino data over much longer periods.

“These results show the potential of KM3NeT/ORCA to test fundamental principles of physics, even with a relatively small detector,” says Lukas Hennig, a PhD student at ECAP and the study’s other corresponding author. “With more data and an expanding detector, we will be able to search for even smaller effects.”

As KM3NeT/ORCA expands toward its full planned configuration, researchers expect to improve their sensitivity to possible deviations from relativity. They also hope to extend these investigations to KM3NeT/ARCA, a detector designed to study much higher-energy neutrinos originating from distant astrophysical sources.

Some proposed violations of Lorentz invariance could become more pronounced as neutrino energy increases or as particles travel across greater distances. Neutrinos arriving from distant cosmic sources may therefore offer a way to test effects too small to detect with atmospheric neutrinos.

articles.title: Rubies on Mars?
articles.dek: Written by Roger C. Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University
paragraphs: Written by Roger C. Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University

Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected. Perseverance is equipped with a fantastic set of instruments for studying the rock record of this ancient planet. Both PIXL and SuperCam have great capabilities for detecting all kinds of elements. SHERLOC, SuperCam, and PIXL can detect minerals using various techniques including x-ray fluorescence, Raman, and infrared spectroscopies. As a side benefit of the way SuperCam performs its Raman spectroscopy, it can also study time-resolved luminescence. Normally luminescence occurs over a broad wavelength range (most of Earth’s commercial lighting uses luminescence in some way or another).

Two years ago, the SuperCam team was startled to find strong, narrow luminescence peaks at two wavelengths of 692. 7 and 694. 1 nanometers when they shot a light-colored rock with the laser. This luminescence comes from delayed atomic transitions in chromium atoms present in a corundum mineral structure. SuperCam can time the delay of the atomic transitions via the resulting photons, and so we could verify that this emission came from chromium in corundum. The results were published in Geophysical Research Letters by a team led by Ann Ollila earlier this year, so you can read all about it. The gemstone version of chromium-containing corundum is ruby.
Prior to installing SuperCam on Perseverance, we placed a ruby in the laser beam and watched the entire room pulse a brilliant red as SuperCam’s laser beam hit the gemstone; it was extremely bright.

While we haven’t found collectable rubies on Mars yet, the little corundum crystals are helping us learn more about Mars’ past. Corundum is a metamorphic and pegmatitic mineral which we would not expect to find on Mars, a planet that lacks plate tectonics. However, large meteor and asteroid impacts can create local metamorphism due to long-term heating from the impact. Because we are in a very ancient terrain near the rim of Jezero crater, we can expect some evidence of localized metamorphism. As the first mission in such terrain, we are learning new things.

Earlier in the mission we tried this technique only rarely; lately we have carried out the time-resolved luminescence observations frequently on light-toned rocks to look for more evidence of impact effects. It’s great to have this unexpected tool on board as we delve further into Mars’ deep past.

articles.title: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?
articles.dek: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University
paragraphs: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University

Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “ Badger Peak .” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported , that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort to add a gabbro, an igneous rock made mostly of calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar and pyroxene crystals, to Perseverance’s sample collection . In search of a new local gabbroic candidate to sample, Perseverance traveled about 100 meters (330 feet) to a different patch of light-toned rocks . Indeed, visual and chemical data from the light-toned rocks in the new workspace revealed a composition similar to that of “Badger Peak.”

To improve the odds of collecting a sample this time, the team made prudent decisions: choosing a neighboring rock with a flatter surface better oriented for the drill stabilizers to press against, and using a coring bit with less wear. At last, in a display of the rover’s namesake quality, the drill made it about 3. 1 centimeters (1. 2 inches) into the rock. Sample acquisition activities followed, making “Singita” the rover’s first sample in more than a year. While Singita is the newest sample, it may be among the oldest rocks in Perseverance’s collection .
Textures in the rock suggest that it likely formed deep in the crust and was modified and excavated by at least one, and possibly multiple, large impact events.

Perseverance has now completed its 66 th successful abrasion and collected an intriguing new sample alongside it. paragraphs: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University

Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “ Badger Peak .” That’s no coincidence. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort to add a gabbro, an igneous rock made mostly of calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar and pyroxene crystals, to Perseverance’s sample collection . articles.title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Prostate Cancer That Could Transform Treatment
articles.dek: A newly identified vulnerability in a cancer-driving protein could pave the way for a different approach to treating prostate cancer.
paragraphs: A newly identified vulnerability in a cancer-driving protein could pave the way for a different approach to treating prostate cancer.

Researchers at the University of Michigan have identified a potential way to target a protein that helps drive prostate cancer but has long been considered beyond the reach of drugs. Their experimental compound, PBITE-1, interfered with the protein’s cancer-promoting activity in laboratory models, offering a possible starting point for more targeted treatments.

The protein, known as ERG, becomes abnormally active when two genes, TMPRSS2 and ERG , fuse together. This genetic rearrangement occurs in roughly half of prostate cancer cases among patients of European ancestry and promotes tumor cell growth and migration.

For years, ERG has been considered “undruggable” because it appeared to lack the molecular pockets where medications typically attach. In the new study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , researchers discovered an accessible pocket in a region called the PNT domain, which helps regulate ERG’s interactions with other proteins.

After screening more than 1,600 compounds, the team identified a promising molecule and refined it into PBITE-1. In experiments involving prostate cancer cell lines and laboratory models of human and mouse prostate tissue, the compound inhibited ERG activity, triggered cancer cell death, and reduced the ability of cancer cells to invade surrounding tissue.

“Although we were the first to identify the gene fusion as a driver of prostate cancer, it was challenging to find a drug target for ERG,” said Arul Chinnaiyan, M. D. , Ph. D. , S. P. Hicks Professor of Pathology and member of the Rogel Cancer Center.

Most existing prostate cancer therapies focus on androgen receptors, proteins that respond to hormones such as testosterone. These receptors can activate the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, helping fuel tumor growth. Drugs that block androgen signaling can slow the disease, but tumors often develop resistance, and treatment can cause side effects that affect quality of life.
Targeting ERG directly could provide an alternative approach for patients whose tumors carry the gene fusion, rather than relying exclusively on treatments that interfere with hormone signaling.
“This work shows that instead of treating all prostate cancer as one disease, we have the potential to personalize therapy for subtypes of prostate cancer.”

PBITE-1 remains an experimental research tool, and its effects have not been established in patients. Further research will be needed to determine whether compounds targeting ERG can be developed into safe and effective medicines.
“Although it is unlikely that PBITE-1 is ready to become a drug any time soon, this study shows that ERG is a druggable target,” Chinnaiyan said.
“It is exciting that we now have a path forward to target ERG in prostate cancer.”

articles.title: A New Approach Could Eliminate “Zombie” Cancer Cells That Survive Chemotherapy
articles.dek: Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by blocking their own self-destruct system, but researchers have found a way to switch it back on and kill those cells.
paragraphs: Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by blocking their own self-destruct system, but researchers have found a way to switch it back on and kill those cells.

Chemotherapy can leave behind cancer cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and capable of helping a tumor recover. These survivors can draw support from an unexpected source, the immune system, by activating responses that normally help the body repair damaged tissue.

This “zombie-like state,” called “premature senescence,” involves dramatic changes. Within a few days of exposure to chemotherapy, senescent cells can grow to almost ten times the size of a normal cell and increase the activity of genes associated with wound healing. Their ability to release inflammatory mediators, molecules that attract immune cells, also increases greatly.

The danger lies in the range of jobs the immune system performs. Alongside protecting against infection, it coordinates the repair and replacement of damaged tissue. During wound healing, it stimulates cell division to replace cells lost through injury and triggers the growth of blood vessels that deliver extra oxygen and nutrients. Normally, this complex, carefully coordinated process ensures that new cells appear only where and when they are needed.

Cancers can exploit those repair functions by masquerading as damaged tissue. Instead of destroying malignant cells, the immune system can then help them divide and obtain more oxygen and nutrients. That behavior has led cancers to be described as “wounds that do not heal,” although how they activate the immune system’s wound-healing capabilities remains poorly understood.

Research newly published in Science Advances identifies a mechanism that helps cancer cells survive chemotherapy and enter senescence. Scientists at the Smurfit Institute of Genetics at Trinity College Dublin found that molecules called Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins, or IAPs, can protect tumor cells from the killing effects of commonly used chemotherapy drugs. The team was led by Professor Seamus Martin, Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics, and Dr. Gokhan Gunay, a postdoctoral research fellow.

The researchers found that DNA damage caused by chemotherapy switched on molecules called “Death Receptors,” which can trigger a cell’s self-destruct program. IAPs neutralized their cell-killing effects. That protection allowed surviving tumor cells to enter senescence, where they could coordinate wound-healing responses that benefit the tumor and help it recover after treatment.

But the cells’ continued survival also depended heavily on IAPs, creating a vulnerability. In the study, compounds called IAP antagonists neutralized these proteins and reactivated the Death Receptor self-destruct program, selectively eliminating the senescent cells. The same proteins that helped the cells escape chemotherapy thus remained essential to keeping them alive afterward.

Senescent cells are also relevant beyond cancer treatment. They accumulate in tissues as people age, and that buildup is thought to contribute to age-related inflammation and declining normal function in many tissues.

For cancer treatment, the findings identify both an escape mechanism and a possible way to target the cells that use it. Tumors that evade chemotherapy remain a major challenge for clinicians, and improved treatments could offer patients better survival and quality of life.
Professor Martin said, “Discovering how tumors can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter senescence is an important and challenging problem.

“These new findings suggest ways in which we may be able to lower the defenses of tumors by neutralizing IAPs after the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, which should block their entry to senescence and kill more cells of the tumor.”

articles.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
articles.dek: There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens.
paragraphs: There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens.
The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration.
It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U. S. has seen only two times in the past half-century.
One was the Newt Gingrich “revolution” in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.
The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals.
In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected.

The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making Gingrich the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House.
It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency .

The combative Gingrich emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm. Confrontations over spending led to controversial government shutdowns and the first modern threat to default on America’s debt obligations .
Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity to win a second term.

In the run-up to his bid for reelection, Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft welfare reform legislation and new bills dealing with crime and immigration . Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s the United States had a balanced budget .
Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when Gingrich pushed for impeachment following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky.
Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, survived his Senate trial . Ironically, it was Gingrich who resigned after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process.
Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized.
Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal produced a Democratic Party victory.

Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote and brought new members to both chambers who were younger, more liberal and reform-minded .

They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the government more open, more honest and more accountable . New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law.
A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, would be elected president two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed.

The post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials.
These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an imperial president .
The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – but not without creating their own problems .

All the post-Watergate presidents thought the war powers resolution was unconstitutional , objecting to its restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and U. S. military interventions overseas continued to occur . Special prosecutors conducted many investigations , but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results.
Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and lost reelection to Ronald Reagan , who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics.
Over time, many presidents, especially Donald Trump , dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms.

paragraphs: Read this release in English here . La NASA busca a los exploradores que ayudarán a escribir el próximo capítulo de los vuelos espaciales tripulados.

Ya está abierto el plazo de inscripción para la próxima promoción de astronautas de la agencia, que se incorporarán a la NASA en un momento en el que Estados Unidos regresa a la Luna, construye la Base Lunar y sienta las bases para las primeras misiones tripuladas a Marte.

La próxima generación de astronautas se entrenará para operar en la superficie lunar, vivir y trabajar fuera de la Tierra, y llevar a cabo misiones que ampliarán los límites de la exploración con seres humanos más lejos que nunca.

Los ciudadanos estadounidenses interesados en formar parte del cuerpo de astronautas tienen hasta las 11:59 p. m. EST (hora del este) del jueves 3 de diciembre para enviar la documentación completa de su solicitud a:

“Este es un momento extraordinario para incorporarse al cuerpo de astronautas de la NASA”, afirmó el administrador de la agencia espacial, Jared Isaacman. “Las personas que seleccionemos podrían pisar la Luna, vivir y trabajar en la Base Lunar, y ayudar a desarrollar los sistemas y operaciones que, en última instancia, llevarán a las tripulaciones a Marte. Esas misiones exigirán excelencia técnica, buen criterio, trabajo en equipo y valentía. El cuerpo de astronautas de la NASA siempre ha recurrido a estadounidenses excepcionales con la disposición de asumir retos extraordinarios al servicio de la nación.
Si quieres unirte a esa tradición, ven a ayudarnos a escribir el próximo capítulo de la mayor aventura de la humanidad”.
La NASA prevé realizar su selección definitiva a finales de 2027 para comenzar la capacitación de la próxima promoción de candidatos a astronautas.

“La ventana de oportunidad está abierta. La misión nos espera. Y lo único que falta en la mayor aventura en la que se ha embarcado la humanidad eres tú”, afirmó Matt Anderson, administrador adjunto de la NASA.

La agencia abrió por última vez la convocatoria en 2024. De entre más de 8. 000 candidaturas, en 2025 se seleccionaron 10 candidatos a astronautas, que actualmente están completando casi dos años de capacitación.

“Para quienes presentan su candidatura, convertirse en astronauta de la NASA es más que una oportunidad profesional”, afirmó Scott Tingle, astronauta jefe y presidente de la Junta de Selección de Astronautas del Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA, en Houston. “Es una oportunidad para formar parte de un legado de exploradores que han ampliado los límites del conocimiento y desempeñar un papel en las misiones que marcarán el futuro de la humanidad en el espacio. La próxima generación de candidatos a astronautas podría ayudar a escribir la historia, al tiempo que inspira a futuros científicos, ingenieros y exploradores”.

Desde la década de 1960, la NASA ha seleccionado a 370 personas para capacitarlas como candidatos a astronautas en sus misiones, cada vez más exigentes. La agencia cuenta actualmente con 32 astronautas en activo, y los candidatos seleccionados se unirán a sus filas para formarse en caminatas espaciales, geología lunar, manejo de aeronaves de alto rendimiento y mucho más.

articles.title: Hidden Brain Signals Could Predict Alzheimer’s Years Before Symptoms Appear
articles.dek: Subtle differences in brain activity may reveal who is most vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease and who could remain mentally sharp well into old age.
paragraphs: Subtle differences in brain activity may reveal who is most vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease and who could remain mentally sharp well into old age.

Distinct patterns of brain activity may predict Alzheimer’s disease years before memory problems or hallmark brain changes appear. Stanford Medicine researchers have developed a scoring system that identifies people at greater risk of cognitive decline while also recognizing those whose brains show unusual resilience to aging.

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances , found that these patterns could predict future cognitive decline more effectively than several established risk indicators, including genetics and Alzheimer’s biomarkers.

Researchers analyzed resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 “super agers,” adults aged 75 and older with memory abilities comparable to those of typical 45-year-olds, and 110 similarly aged people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease.

“Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine. “Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.”

The team identified distinct patterns of activity across brain networks and developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score. The system distinguished super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers tested the ARC score in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. Although participants initially showed no clear differences in cognitive performance, their brain activity patterns predicted different outcomes over follow-up periods extending as long as 12 years.

People with more Alzheimer’s-like activity experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid-beta plaques or receive an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. Those with super-ager-like patterns generally maintained stronger cognitive abilities.

“We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease,” said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a Stanford postdoctoral scholar and lead author.

“We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer’s field nowadays — most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease,” Zhang said. “What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.”

The ARC score performed as well as or better than existing biomarkers at predicting progression toward Alzheimer’s, while offering information at an earlier stage. Combining the score with traditional biomarkers improved predictions further.

“We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer’s disease,” Zhao said. “Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.”
The researchers also found a relationship between ARC scores and brain age, a broader measure of aging derived from functional MRI data.

“I’m excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline,” Zhang said.

articles.title: NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts
articles.dek: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.
paragraphs: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.

A new study , published Monday in the latest issue of The Astrophysical Journal, details the discovery of a previously hidden companion object that keeps pulling material away from the massive star every 113 days as they orbit one another. This partner is either a stellar-mass black hole, or the dense collapsed core of a massive star called a neutron star.
This is the first X-ray detection of one of this class of erupting stars. It is also the first of these objects found with a black hole or neutron star companion.

The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the mass of this star is at least 33 times that of the Sun.

“For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,” said Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, who led this study. “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen.”

The star AT 2016blu is a type of luminous blue variable, which are hot, massive stars characterized by changes in brightness. Eta Carinae, for example, is a particularly well-known luminous blue variable. ) AT 2016blu is a special type of luminous blue variable that undergoes rapid and repeated increases in brightness. The spikes in brightness are so extreme that they resemble supernova explosions, where a massive star collapses onto itself and material then hurtles outward into space. However, unlike in a supernova explosion, the star is not destroyed, so AT 2016blu is also referred to as a “supernova impostor.”
Between 2012 and 2026, astronomers detected at least 27 bursts of optical light, or light in wavelengths that are visible to our eyes, from AT 2016blu roughly every 113 days.

“This star’s behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly it’s not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,” said co-author Núria Torres-Albà, also of the University of Virginia. “To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data, timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst.”
The team used Chandra because it is the only X-ray telescope with sharp enough vision to distinguish AT 2016blu from another nearby bright X-ray source.

“We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,” said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. “The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.”

Chandra data from March 2026 revealed that AT 2016blu was at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in Chandra data from 2001 to 2002, which is before the outbursts began. The best explanation for this is that material from the star is falling onto a neutron star or black hole during the closest approach in their oval-shaped orbit around one another. When they come close together, material ejected by the star gets captured by the black hole or neutron star. The material orbits at very high speeds close to the speed of light, getting so hot that it shines brightly in X-rays.

AT 2016blu is bright enough in X-rays to be classified as a candidate of ultra-luminous X-ray source. These are rare, bright X-ray sources found with telescopes like Chandra that astronomers have yet to fully understand. Scientists’ current thinking is that some of them contain neutron stars, and others have black holes.

These new observations suggest there could be a link between ultra-luminous X-ray sources and the kind of violent stellar eruptions seen in AT 2016blu, especially because many ultra-luminous X-ray sources undergo large changes in X-ray brightness.

The discovery of this system may also help studies of stars that change in brightness before they undergo supernova explosions. Astronomers suspect that much of this behavior may be caused by systems containing a massive star orbiting a compact object or another massive star.

“For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,” said Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, who led this study. “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen.”

The star AT 2016blu is a type of luminous blue variable, which are hot, massive stars characterized by changes in brightness. Eta Carinae, for example, is a particularly well-known luminous blue variable. ) AT 2016blu is a special type of luminous blue variable that undergoes rapid and repeated increases in brightness. The spikes in brightness are so extreme that they resemble supernova explosions, where a massive star collapses onto itself and material then hurtles outward into space. However, unlike in a supernova explosion, the star is not destroyed, so AT 2016blu is also referred to as a “supernova impostor.”
Between 2012 and 2026, astronomers detected at least 27 bursts of optical light, or light in wavelengths that are visible to our eyes, from AT 2016blu roughly every 113 days.

“This star’s behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly it’s not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,” said co-author Núria Torres-Albà, also of the University of Virginia. “To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data, timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst.”
The team used Chandra because it is the only X-ray telescope with sharp enough vision to distinguish AT 2016blu from another nearby bright X-ray source.

“We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,” said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. “The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.”

Chandra data from March 2026 revealed that AT 2016blu was at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in Chandra data from 2001 to 2002, which is before the outbursts began. The best explanation for this is that material from the star is falling onto a neutron star or black hole during the closest approach in their oval-shaped orbit around one another. When they come close together, material ejected by the star gets captured by the black hole or neutron star. The material orbits at very high speeds close to the speed of light, getting so hot that it shines brightly in X-rays.

AT 2016blu is bright enough in X-rays to be classified as a candidate of ultra-luminous X-ray source. These are rare, bright X-ray sources found with telescopes like Chandra that astronomers have yet to fully understand. Scientists’ current thinking is that some of them contain neutron stars, and others have black holes.

These new observations suggest there could be a link between ultra-luminous X-ray sources and the kind of violent stellar eruptions seen in AT 2016blu, especially because many ultra-luminous X-ray sources undergo large changes in X-ray brightness.

The discovery of this system may also help studies of stars that change in brightness before they undergo supernova explosions. Astronomers suspect that much of this behavior may be caused by systems containing a massive star orbiting a compact object or another massive star.

articles.title: La NASA destina un millón de dólares al reto estudiantil Base Lunar
articles.dek: Read this release in English here . El domingo 8 de noviembre de 2026, la NASA anunció la convocatoria del reto estudiantil Base Lunar, dotado con un millón de dólares,…
paragraphs: Read this release in English here . El domingo 8 de noviembre de 2026, la NASA anunció la convocatoria del reto estudiantil Base Lunar, dotado con un millón de dólares, durante un acto de MAX POWER celebrado en el Complejo de Visitantes del Centro Espacial Kennedy, en Florida. En el marco de una edad de oro de la ciencia, la competición invita a equipos de estudiantes de escuelas secundarias y centros de educación superior de Estados Unidos a aportar diseños para la Base Lunar.

“Buscamos estudiantes dispuestos a pensar de forma creativa, a trabajar en equipo y a abordar problemas reales relacionados con el futuro de la NASA en la Luna”, dijo el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman. “No hace falta esperar hasta la graduación para contribuir. La curiosidad, la creatividad y la voluntad de afrontar problemas difíciles sin respuestas obvias son precisamente las cualidades que necesitamos mientras construimos lo que viene a continuación”.

La NASA está construyendo la Base Lunar, donde los astronautas vivirán, trabajarán y explorarán la región del Polo Sur lunar. La presencia humana permanente en la Luna allana el camino para futuras misiones tripuladas a Marte y requiere talento procedente de diversos sectores y ámbitos.

“A medida que construimos y diseñamos los cimientos de la Base Lunar, queremos aprovechar todo el ingenio y la innovación para tener en cuenta cada aspecto que nuestros exploradores puedan necesitar para vivir y trabajar allí”, afirmó Carlos García-Galán, director del programa Base Lunar. “Los estudiantes aportan precisamente las ideas audaces que estamos buscando, y estoy deseando descubir su enfoque. En definitiva, la Base Lunar es para ellos, las personas que vivirán en un mundo en el que los seres humanos estarán en la Luna para quedarse”.

Este reto, que consta de varias fases, refuerza el compromiso de la NASA con el desarrollo de las competencias técnicas del personal aeroespacial del futuro. Los equipos de estudiantes diseñarán soluciones innovadoras para la Base Lunar en seis categorías: generación y almacenamiento de energía, construcción, sistemas de soporte vital, movilidad en la superficie, redes de comunicaciones y seguridad de los astronautas. La iniciativa ofrece a los participantes la oportunidad de adquirir las aptitudes necesarias para una carrera en la industria espacial, al tiempo que contribuye al avance de nuevos conceptos tecnológicos para la Base Lunar.
Los participantes deben inscribirse en el reto a través de la plataforma NASA STEM Gateway , en inglés. El plazo de inscripción está abierto hasta el 25 de enero de 2027.

“Los estudiantes son la siguiente generación de exploradores e innovadores. Sus perspectivas únicas son fundamentales para ayudarnos a imaginar un futuro lejos de la Tierra, y me entusiasma ver la creatividad y el ingenio que suscitará este reto”, dijo Elaine Ho, administradora asociada de la Oficina de Participación en STEM de la sede central de la NASA en Washington.

El reto estudiantil Base Lunar aborda parámetros medioambientales y de diseño de misiones reales para la vida y las operaciones en la superficie lunar. Los trabajos solicitados reflejan destrezas propias del sector (estudios comparativos, propuestas conceptuales y presentaciones a las partes interesadas), lo que permite a los participantes de formación técnica, profesional y de diversas ramas académicas desarrollar capacidades relevantes para su carrera sin necesidad de contar con experiencia previa en ingeniería o en el ámbito técnico.

La Oficina de Participación en STEM diseñó el reto en colaboración con el programa Base Lunar. El Institute of Competition Sciences (Instituto de Ciencias de la Competición) lo gestiona mediante un contrato con el Centro de Excelencia de la NASA para la Innovación Colaborativa, dependiente de la Dirección de Misiones de Investigación y Tecnología de la agencia.
Para obtener información detallada y en inglés sobre el reto, los requisitos de participación y las bases oficiales, visita:

articles.title: Smithsonian Scientists Built a Virtual Universe 1.5 Billion Light-Years Across
articles.dek: Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in a record-breaking simulation that could reveal new secrets about the Big Bang and the birth of galaxies.
paragraphs: Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in a record-breaking simulation that could reveal new secrets about the Big Bang and the birth of galaxies.

Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in extraordinary detail using one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. The enormous simulation, called “Lumina,” allows researchers to explore how the earliest stars and galaxies formed, how dark matter influenced their development, and how radiation transformed the young cosmos.

Developed by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Lumina is among the largest and most sophisticated simulations of the early universe ever produced. It provides a virtual record of cosmic evolution that scientists can compare with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope.

The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society , could help answer fundamental questions about what happened after the Big Bang. By recreating the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation, scientists can test whether their current theories accurately describe the early universe or whether surprising telescope discoveries point to physics that remains unexplained.

Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing theories to explain the origins of stars, galaxies, and the enormous structures that fill the universe. Modern supercomputers have added a powerful new approach by allowing scientists to simulate how the cosmos should develop if those theories are correct.

These simulations act as virtual laboratories. Researchers can start with conditions in the young universe, apply the known laws of physics, and calculate how matter and energy evolve over billions of years. The results can then be compared with actual telescope observations.

If the simulated universe resembles what astronomers observe, it strengthens confidence in the underlying models. But if important differences emerge, those discrepancies could reveal missing pieces in our understanding of cosmic history.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”

Lumina sets a new benchmark for a particular class of cosmological simulations known as radiation hydrodynamics simulations. These models calculate how gas, dark matter, and radiation influence one another as the universe develops, making it possible to investigate the processes responsible for creating the earliest galaxies.

Dark matter is an invisible form of matter whose gravitational influence helps shape galaxies and other cosmic structures. Meanwhile, radiation from stars and other luminous objects affects the surrounding gas, changing its temperature and physical state. Capturing these interactions is essential for understanding how the early universe evolved.

Lumina follows these processes across the first 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how young galaxies formed and how their light gradually altered the enormous clouds of gas that filled the space between them.

The simulation’s scale is particularly remarkable. It encompasses a cube of space approximately 1. 5 billion light-years along each side, representing more than 100 times the volume covered by previous comparable simulations. That enormous region is similar in scale to the volumes of the universe astronomers can investigate with today’s most advanced telescopes.
One of Lumina’s most important advances involves a process called reionization, which fundamentally changed the gas that filled the early universe.

As the first generations of luminous objects emerged, their radiation stripped electrons from atoms of hydrogen and helium, transforming much of the surrounding gas into an ionized state. This transition helped establish the conditions found throughout the universe today.

articles.title: MAX POWER: NASA’s Inaugural Aerospace Expo Ignites America’s Future
articles.dek: Thousands gathered over several days in early November to experience MAX POWER – NASA’s first exhibition of America’s superiority in space, aeronautics, and technology on and…
paragraphs: Thousands gathered over several days in early November to experience MAX POWER – NASA’s first exhibition of America’s superiority in space, aeronautics, and technology on and around the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The multi-day, family-friendly event honored the nation’s 250th anniversary and served as a culmination of the agency’s Inspiration Tour .

Among the many highlights, NASA welcomed President Donald J. Trump to MAX POWER, which featured flyovers and a skydive from NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and announced a new X-plane, astronaut candidate recruitment, a student Moon Base challenge, and discussed the agency’s latest lunar exploration plans.

“It was a great week at NASA Kennedy, where we were joined by the President and federal, state, international, and industry leaders,” said Isaacman. “During our nation’s 250th birthday, the year of Artemis II’s voyage around the Moon, we were thrilled to invite the public out to see the rockets, the landers, the rovers, and the technology that will return astronauts to the lunar surface and build the base, not to mention witness a wonderful airshow that included NASA research aircraft and was headlined by the U. S. Air Force Thunderbirds.”

Through multiple park experiences, NASA and external collaborators at UP. Summit, Air Dot Show, Purpose Entertainment, and Delaware North each hosted a variety of private and public events Nov. 4-8. Teams showcased the newest aircraft, rovers, autonomous vehicles, and technologies defining the future of air and space. Astronauts, scientists, engineers, pilots, and subject matter experts were on hand for a variety of moderated discussions, appearances, and more.
Some of the key announcements made at MAX POWER included:

While guests journeyed between three park locations on the ground at NASA Kennedy’s historic Shuttle Landing Facility, T-38s, F-5s, and an ER-2 sped overhead during four flyovers, several of which were piloted by Isaacman. Some guests also were invited to a black-tie gala featuring agency leadership remarks and panel discussions with Apollo and Artemis astronauts.

NASA’s Artemis III crew members also took to the stage during the astronaut announcement, previewing their test flight in low Earth orbit in 2027. NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, and Andre Douglas, as well as ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano all will fly aboard Orion, will launch on the SLS (Space Launch System), to test docking and rendezvous capabilities with the Blue Origin Blue Moon lander and SpaceX Starship lunar lander test articles, respectively, laying the groundwork to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028.

Finally, while this expo was the first for NASA, there is much more to come. As part of a public/private partnership, NASA and its partners also announced CAPEWEEK: The Great American Aerospace and Technology Expo at Kennedy. The new annual expo will debut March 27 through April 2, 2028, at Kennedy’s Shuttle Landing Facility, with a footprint expected to ultimately grow upward of 500,000 people.

“It was an educational and inspirational event, with a student Moon Base science challenge, a call for more NASA astronauts, and the unveiling of a new X-plane,” said Isaacman. “All credit goes to the NASA workforce and our partners, doing the work each day to bring the NASA missions to reality, and events like this so successful. So much so that we are doing it again, only bigger. CAPEWEEK begins in 2028.”
